headline: High-risk default write/egress pairing: AutoGen can execute code and write files while Chatwoot handles customer data, creating leakage and compliance exposure if connected without isolation.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: AutoGen can read/write files and execute shell commands, so if Chatwoot content is bridged into its workspace, prompt-like content could influence downstream tool use. Chatwoot exposes customer-facing messages and integrations, but no direct shared channel is documented. The pathway exists via shared files or copied content, so I rate it medium rather than low.
conditions: IF Chatwoot outputs are copied into an AutoGen working directory
IF AutoGen agents treat file contents as instructions or tool directives
mitigations: Keep Chatwoot exports out of AutoGen workspaces
Use a read-only handoff file format
Strip instructions from customer text before ingestion
Require human review before any AutoGen tool call
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all bridged messages

B_data_leakage.rationale: AutoGen has broad network egress and handles model provider API keys; Chatwoot touches customer data, contact profiles, orders, and messages. If Chatwoot data is fed into AutoGen, the pair can leak sensitive customer content to third-party model providers in default configurations. The blast radius includes multiple work products and potentially regulated data.
conditions: IF customer messages or orders are passed from Chatwoot into AutoGen
IF AutoGen uses configured external model providers
mitigations: Disable external model providers for sensitive runs
Redact customer identifiers before transfer
Use a local-only model backend
Limit AutoGen to synthetic or public data
requires-engineering: enforce DLP on the handoff path

C_capability_conflict.rationale: AutoGen can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses; Chatwoot is a customer-support system with API integrations and reports. If both operate on the same mutable workspace or shared files, they can overwrite each other's artifacts or race on state. The profiles do not show locking, so overlapping write surfaces create a default conflict risk.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or shared artifact store
IF Chatwoot exports are edited by AutoGen and re-imported
mitigations: Assign separate working directories
Make shared artifacts read-only
Serialize writes through one orchestrator
Avoid concurrent edits to the same ticket export
requires-engineering: add file locks or transactional storage

D_cascading_error.rationale: AutoGen is a multi-agent orchestration framework that can generate outputs from tool use, and Chatwoot can surface those outputs in customer-support workflows. If Chatwoot treats AutoGen-generated text as authoritative, errors can cascade into customer-facing replies or reports. Because the pair lacks documented verification between them, the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF AutoGen-generated text is inserted into Chatwoot replies or reports
IF Chatwoot operators do not verify the generated content before sending
mitigations: Require human approval before sending replies
Mark AI-generated text as untrusted
Add citation checks for factual claims
Use templates instead of free-form generation
requires-engineering: build verification gates in Chatwoot

E_compliance.rationale: Chatwoot touches customer data, contact profiles, and interaction history, while AutoGen handles model-provider API keys and broad network egress. If customer data flows into AutoGen, residency and retention obligations can be violated by external model processing or logging. The profiles do not show matching compliance controls, so the pair is high risk.
conditions: IF customer data from Chatwoot is sent to external model providers through AutoGen
IF retention or residency requirements apply to that customer data
mitigations: Exclude regulated records from the workflow
Use a local deployment for model inference
Minimize logged payloads
Document retention and deletion handling
requires-engineering: perform a formal DPA/residency review
